title: Load Securing: The Basics
whatItIs: All loads must be secure, whatever the vehicle, the load or the length of the journey. The securing system has to hold the load when you brake, corner or swerve.

keyFacts.text: Operators, drivers and consignors MUST secure all loads and make sure they're loaded, carried and unloaded safely.
The securing system MUST withstand the full load weight forwards, and half of it to the sides and to the rear.

keyFacts: Don't rely on a load's weight to keep it in place: friction between most loads and load beds is low.

keyFacts.text: A sheet or net only contains a load. It MUST be used with other securing, such as lashings.

keyFacts: Keep the load near the centre line with its centre of gravity low. Put heavier items at the bottom.

onTheTest.question: A load securing system must withstand a force equal to how much of the load's weight in the forward direction?
onTheTest.why: The minimum is the entire weight of the load forwards, and half the weight to the sides and to the rear.

onTheTest.question: Before you set off, you have doubts about how the consignor has secured your load. What should you do?
options: Drive slowly to the delivery point
Don't set off: report your concerns
Put a sheet over the load
Set off and check it after an hour
onTheTest.why: You should not proceed with a load if you have any doubts about its security. Report concerns to your employer or the load consignor.

traps: Too heavy to move by hand? It can still slide once the vehicle is moving.
Check restraints during the journey: straps and chains can lose tension and loads like sand can settle.
An insecure load can be careless or dangerous driving, for the driver, consignor and operator.
